answers.text: Always three lines in the same order: drop-off time, pallet count, and any damage noted. Time is just the time, pallet count is just the number, and damage is either what's noted or 'none reported' — if the message doesn't mention one of these at all, write 'not given' instead of skipping the line. That keeps it the same every time.

List each call entry as time, customer, topic and outcome, in the order they came in, and then count how many have an outcome marked 'needs follow-up' for the total at the end. If the same customer appears twice in one day for the same topic, count it as one entry, not two, and note that it repeated.

There's an error in this note, and it's not about the crew size or the access time — it's the finishing date. Access is confirmed from 8am on the 22nd and the job is six hours, so it should finish that same afternoon, not the next day on the 23rd as it says.
9 late out of 118 is right, about 92%. But 96 up to 118 is closer to 23%, not the 20% they wrote.

I would sign off on the second one, with 827 and 940 written out. The first one just gives 88% without showing the ticket counts behind it. It could still be correct on its own, but there's no way to check it without running the numbers again.

I would send Email 2, the one with the actual volume numbers and the PO log reference. Email 1 just says 'we'd expect a better rate' without saying what that's based on, so there's nothing there to check. That doesn't mean Email 1 is wrong, I just wouldn't send it without the numbers behind it first.
1. No, not until the tool is approved. 2. Yes. 3. No, that draft hasn't been released. 4. No, better to leave it out. 5. No, that's an employee's home address, personal.

The hourly rates and retainer cap I would not paste straight into the tool, I'd want to take those out first. The non-disclosure clause names both us and the client, so that also needs care. The service scope on its own is fine to include, there's nothing sensitive in what work is being done.

Before it goes to the depot manager each month-end, I would check the stock totals in the AI summary against the actual warehouse counts directly. That way, if a number has been invented or dropped, it shows up straight away, not just a wording mistake.

Reading the invoice and pulling the numbers out is the step I'd worry about most, since everything downstream depends on it. But the real gate should sit at step four, before the payment approval goes out automatically, because once it's submitted the money has moved.
